lesson.focus: Building words from syllable cards (na-ma, ta-ma-ti): hearing the sounds in each syllable, placing the cards, blending to read

summary_en: An edited Funda Wande film of shared word building in Sesotho: the teacher says a word, the class names the first sound and the sounds inside each syllable, and a learner at the board picks and places syllable cards for nama and then tamati. The class reads each word back in chorus, slowly and then faster, one learner reads nama alone, and the clip ends by linking tamati to cooking at home (a turn the transcript labels 'Trainer', so it may be narration). It does not show a sound warm-up, every learner building with their own cards, written practice or fast word recognition; an unrehearsed lesson would also need to show those, and how the teacher checks learners beyond the two at the board. The learners' 'Nna' and the teacher's 'Mma' around nama may be transcription slips for na and ma, so no blockage is built on them.
scope_en: Rumi coached only what the recording shows in class (the teacher and learners). Narration over the film is in the transcript but is not treated as evidence that a step happened. The recording is an edited training film, so a step it does not show may still have happened.

steps.name: Ho futhumatsa ka modumo
steps.name_en: Oral warm-up that foregrounds the sound
steps.note_en: The clip opens on settling the class (look at me, breathe) and goes straight to word building; no rhyme, song or sound game is shown, which may be an edit.

steps.name: Ho tsebisa modumo o motjha
steps.name_en: Introduce the sound and its letters
steps.note_en: No single new sound is introduced; the teacher names the sounds inside each syllable (n and a, tl and a) as learners pick cards, but there is no explicit modelling of articulation or link to a sound chart.

evidence.quote: Ha o re na, ke n le eng?
evidence.en: When you say na, it is n and what?

evidence.quote: O utloa tl le a. Kgetha tl le a.
evidence.en: You hear tl and a. Choose tl and a.

steps.name: Ho kopanya le ho arola medumo
steps.note_en: Learners segment syllables into sounds and blend the syllables back into the word, slow then faster; most of it is in chorus, with a few individual answers from the learner at the board.

evidence.quote: Ha ke re nama, o utlwa modumo ofe o qalang?
evidence.en: When I say nama, which starting sound do you hear?

evidence.quote: Ha re re ma, ho latela eng le eng?
evidence.en: When we say ma, what and what follows?

evidence.quote: Ke batla re le bitse re potlakile jwale.
evidence.en: I want us to say it quickly now.

steps.name: Ho bala le ho aha mantswe a nang le modumo
steps.name_en: Read and build words with the sound
steps.note_en: Two words are built with syllable cards by two learners at the board and one learner reads nama alone; the rest of the class reads back in chorus.

evidence.quote: Tlo o tlo tla o re bopela lentswe la rona la nama.
evidence.en: Come, you will come and build for us our word of nama.

evidence.quote: Ke kopa [learner] yena fela a bue, ne?
evidence.en: I ask that [learner] only should speak, right?

evidence.quote: Tamati.
evidence.en: Tamati.

steps.name: Ho ikwetlisa le ho hlahloba
steps.note_en: No independent practice, workbook or copying of the words is shown; the clip ends on a link to the meaning of tamati.

culture.name: Ho nka karolo ha baithuti bohle
culture.note_en: Choral answers dominate; the teacher picks from raised hands and two learners come to the board, one of whom also reads alone.

evidence.quote: Tlhola letsogo ke tla ikgethela gore na ke tla kgetha mang.
evidence.en: Raise your hand, I will choose for myself who I will choose.

evidence.quote: Ta-ma-ti.
evidence.en: Ta-ma-ti.

culture.name: Ho babatsa boiteko le monahano
culture.note_en: Praise is warm but generic: a class clap for the learner and a thank-you to the class; no praise names the thinking or strategy used.

evidence.quote: Opela [learner] matsoho.
evidence.en: Clap hands for [learner].

evidence.quote: Re lebohile.
evidence.en: Thank you.

culture.name: Ho sebetsana le diphoso
culture.note_en: When the board learner says only 'and a' for tla, the teacher supplies tl at once; on 'and m' the teacher re-asks the question, which is a small probe, then again completes the answer.

evidence.quote: Le a.
evidence.en: And a.

evidence.quote: O utloa tl le a.
evidence.en: You hear tl and a.

evidence.quote: Na ho latela tl?
evidence.en: Does tl follow?

culture.name: Lebelo le tshebediso ya nako
culture.note_en: Pace is brisk and purposeful: two words built and read back in about four and a half minutes with quick moves between them; the film is edited, so dead time cannot be judged.

evidence.quote: Tlohella re tlo etsa lentswe le leng hape hape.
evidence.en: Let's go on to make another word again and again.

evidence.quote: Ke batla re le bitse re potlakile jwale.
evidence.en: I want us to say it quickly now.

culture.name: Ho hlahloba kutlwisiso ya moithuti ka mong
culture.note_en: One learner is checked individually on reading nama and asked to say it more clearly; the board learners are checked as they build; no wider check of individuals is shown.

evidence.quote: Ha re e bale, [learner], ke?
evidence.en: When we read it, [learner], it is?

evidence.quote: Le bitse hantle, ke eng?
evidence.en: Pronounce it well, what is it?

positives.en: The teacher has learners listen for the first sound of a whole word before anything is placed, then splits the syllable into its sounds (na is n and a), so the cards are chosen by ear, not by guessing.
The class is asked to check the board learner's work (which sound did you put?), which keeps the watching learners thinking while one learner builds.
Blending moves from syllable by syllable to faster to a whole word (ta, ma, ti then tamati), the slow-to-fast pattern of the routine, and the learners land on the word themselves.
The teacher hears one learner read nama alone and asks for it again more clearly, a real individual check rather than only the chorus.

blockages.en: When the board learner heard only 'and a' in tla, the teacher said 'tl and a' straight away. The learner did not get to hear the tl sound for themself, so a gap with a two-letter sound stays hidden. Catch-up: say tla slowly, ask what they hear at the very start, let the learner or a partner find the tl card, then ask the learner to say tla again.

Only two learners build at the board and one reads alone; everyone else answers in chorus, and the teacher says ta-ma-ti already split instead of letting learners find the syllables. The teacher cannot tell which learners can segment and build. Catch-up: after the shared word, every learner builds the same word with their own syllable cards (or on a slate) while the teacher walks around and listens to three or four learners each day.

level_of_change.en: Focus skill: moving from shared building at the board to every learner building and being checked. The teacher already wants individual voices (asks one learner to read alone and to say it clearly) but the clip shows no way of getting every learner to build, so level 2 fits; one edited film is thin evidence (low confidence). Coach move: demonstrate the independent word-building step with own cards in this class, then plan it together step by step.

goal.lang: Mo bekeng tse pedi tse tlang, morao ho ho bopa lentswe le mong letlapeng, moithuti e mong le e mong o bopa lentswe leo ka dikarete tsa hae, mme o mamela baithuti ba bararo kapa ba bane ka letsatsi.
goal.en: Over the next two weeks, after building one word at the board, every learner builds that word with their own cards, and you listen to three or four learners a day.

reality.lang: Hona jwale baithuti ba babedi ba bopa letlapeng, e mong o bala a le mong, mme ba bang ba araba hammoho.
reality.en: Right now two learners build at the board, one reads alone, and the others answer together.

options.lang: Moithuti e mong le e mong a be le dikarete tsa dinoko; kapa ba sebetse ka bobedi ka sete e le nngwe; kapa ba ngole lentswe lebatong la bona; o tsamaye ka hare ho tlelase o mamele.
options.en: Each learner has a set of syllable cards; or pairs share one set; or they write the word on their slate; you walk around and listen.

way_forward.lang: Re tla lokisa dikarete hammoho, ke tla bontsha mohato ona tlelaseng ya hao hang, ebe o o leka, re kopane hape ka mora beke.
way_forward.en: We prepare the cards together, I demonstrate the step once in your class, then you try it, and we meet again after a week.

questions.lang: Ha moithuti a re le a ka tla, o ne o nahana eng ka seo a se utlwileng? Ho ne ho ka etsahala eng ha a ne a ka mamela hape?
questions.en: When the learner said 'and a' for tla, what did you think they had heard? What might have happened if they had listened again?

questions.lang: Ha o ne o bitsa tamati ka dinoko, o tseba jwang hore ke baithuti bafe ba ka arolang lentswe leo ba le bang?
questions.en: When you said tamati in syllables, how do you know which learners could split that word on their own?

questions.lang: Ha moithuti a le mong a bala nama, o ithutile eng ka yena? O ka utlwa jwang baithuti ba bang ka tsela eo?
questions.en: When one learner read nama alone, what did you learn about them? How could you hear other learners that way?

debrief_plan.coach_says: Ke a leboha ha o ntumetse ho shebella ho bopa mantswe. Na nka arolelana le wena seo ke se boneng?
debrief_plan.en: Thank you for letting me watch the word building. May I share with you what I saw?

debrief_plan.coach_says: Ke bone o botsa baithuti hore ba utlwa modumo ofe o qalang ho nama, mme ba bala tamati butle, ebe ka potlako. Hape ke bone hore ha moithuti a re le a ka tla, o mo file tl hang hang, mme ke baithuti ba babedi feela ba bopileng.
debrief_plan.en: I saw you ask the learners which sound they hear first in nama, and they read tamati slowly, then quickly. I also saw that when a learner said 'and a' for tla, you gave tl straight away, and only two learners built.

debrief_plan.coach_says: Ha re fa karabo kapele, moithuti ha a utlwe tl ka bowena. Mme ha ba bang ba araba hammoho feela, ha re tsebe hore ke mang ya sa kgoneng ho bopa.
debrief_plan.en: When we give the answer quickly, the learner does not hear tl for themself. And when the others only answer together, we do not know who cannot build yet.

debrief_plan.coach_says: Ke kopa ho utlwa maikutlo a hao. O bona jwang nako eo ya tla, mme ke eng e etsang hore ho be thata hore bohle ba bope?
debrief_plan.en: I would like to hear your view. How do you see that moment with tla, and what makes it hard for everyone to build?

debrief_plan.coach_says: Na re ka lokisa dikarete hore moithuti e mong le e mong a bope lentswe ka bo yena ka mora letlapa? Ke tla o bontsha hang, wena o leke, re kopane hape bekeng e tlang.
debrief_plan.en: Could we prepare cards so that every learner builds the word on their own after the board? I will show you once, you try it, and we meet again next week.

next_step.lang: Ka mora ho bopa lentswe letlapeng, moithuti e mong le e mong a bope lentswe leo ka dikarete tsa hae, mme o mamele baithuti ba bararo kapa ba bane.
next_step.en: After building the word at the board, every learner builds the same word with their own cards, and you listen to three or four learners.

voice.script: Ke a leboha ka thuto ena ya ho bopa mantswe. Ke ratile ha o kopa baithuti ho mamela modumo o qalang pele ba kgetha karete. Ke ratile hape ha le bala tamati butle, ebe ka potlako, ho fihlela ba bitsa lentswe lohle ba le bang. Ntho e le nngwe eo re ka e shebang ke hore ha moithuti a ne a utlwa feela a ho tla, o mo file tl kapele, mme ke baithuti ba babedi feela ba bopileng letlapeng. Kahoo ha re tsebe hore na ba bang ba kgona ho utlwa le ho bopa ka bo bona. Mohato o latelang ke hore ka mora ho bopa letlapeng, moithuti e mong le e mong a bope lentswe leo ka dikarete tsa hae, wena o tsamaye o mamele ba bararo kapa ba bane. O se o ntse o etsa mosebetsi o motle, mme baithuti ba hao ba thabela ho bopa.
voice.en: Thank you for this word-building lesson. I liked that you asked the learners to listen for the first sound before they chose a card. I also liked that you read tamati slowly, then quickly, until they said the whole word themselves. One thing we can look at is that when a learner heard only the a in tla, you gave them tl quickly, and only two learners built at the board. So we do not know whether the others can hear and build on their own. The next step is that after building at the board, every learner builds that word with their own cards, and you walk around and listen to three or four. You are already doing good work, and your learners enjoy building.

grounding.display: 20 of 20 of Rumi's longer quotes (4+ words) are word for word in the turn Rumi cited
grounding.note_en: Counted on Rumi's own quotes before any fix. Only quotes found word for word in the transcript on this page are published; each links to the moment it was said.

coverage.display: 22 of 22 report items filled with evidence or a reason

stability.label: measured
stability.display: The three readings agreed on what they saw in 12 of 15 items

accuracy.label: measured
accuracy.line: These numbers measure Rumi: whether its quotes are really in the lesson, whether it filled every part of the report, and whether it reads the lesson the same way three times. They do not grade the teacher.

model: Lesson-step and classroom-culture judgements by Claude Opus 5.5, the stricter of the two models we compared. Three independent readings of the same transcript; the report shows the median reading, with each item's status taken from the majority.

routine.name: Ho kopanya dinoko hore e be lentswe
routine.note_en: Learners say the syllables one at a time, then faster, then as one word (ta, ma, ti to tamati); done in chorus, and the recording does not show a finger running under the cards.

evidence.quote: Ta, ma, ti.
evidence.en: Ta, ma, ti.

evidence.quote: Ke batla re le bitse re potlakile jwale.
evidence.en: I want us to say it quickly now.

evidence.quote: Tamati.
evidence.en: Tamati.

routine.name: Ho arola lentswe ka dinoko
routine.name_en: Segmenting a said word into syllables
routine.note_en: The teacher says the word already split (ta-ma-ti) and supplies the syllables; learners name sounds within syllables but are not asked to find the syllables of a said word themselves.

evidence.quote: re tlo etsa lentswe la ta-ma-ti.
evidence.en: we are going to make the word of ta-ma-ti.

evidence.quote: Tla, ma, ti. Ho latela eng?
evidence.en: Tla, ma, ti. What follows?

routine.name: Ho aha mantswe mmoho
routine.note_en: The shared-building routine is clear: a learner comes to the board, the teacher says the word, asks what comes first and next, the learner finds and places the cards, and the class is asked what was placed; the teacher sometimes gives the answer before the learner finds it.

evidence.quote: O shebe medumo ya hao, o kgethe na.
evidence.en: Look at your sounds, choose na.

evidence.quote: Ba nthetseng, modumo o o beileng ke ofeng?
evidence.en: Look at me, which sound did you put?

evidence.quote: Lentsu la rona ke leo jwale le se le feletse.
evidence.en: Our word is that one now it is complete.

routine.name: Ho aha mantswe o le mong
routine.note_en: Every learner building the words with their own cards, and copying them into books, is not shown in this clip.

routine.name: Ho bala mantswe a hahilweng kapele
routine.name_en: Reading the built words back, fast
routine.note_en: No fast reading of the week's words in changing order is shown.

routine_note_en: Extra lens for this partner's recordings: the steps of their word-building and phonics routine.
